Messages.Author: Emiliano Imeroni
Messages.Body:
Hi all,

I have some curiosities related to tournament/qualifier rules.
I guess the right place to ask would be the Princes'
Conclave, but I'm not a Prince so here we are :-P

Any help is appreciated, even better if "official" (Oscar?
LSJ?).

1) Consider the situation in which a player who has
played all the preliminary rounds and has qualified to
play the final has to leave without playing the final.

What happens to his ranking in the tournament?
Sections 3.1.4 and 3.3.2 of the V:EKN tournament rules
do not entirely clarify the matter to me.

This issue becomes of particular relevance in a Qualifier
tournament. For instance, suppose there are 6 qualification
"slots", and the player who has ended the preliminary rounds
being 4th in the ranking cannot play the final round. Does he
qualify or not? And what happens in the same situation if,
say, the qualification slots are only 4?

2) One more question about qualifier rules.
Is it possible for a player to declare before the tournament
starts that he does not wish to qualify, and then be treated
the same way as an "already qualified" player (i.e. not
counting towards the number of qualification slots)?

Thanks a lot!

Greets,
Emiliano

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Emiliano Imeroni wrote:
> 1) Consider the situation in which a player who has
> played all the preliminary rounds and has qualified to
> play the final has to leave without playing the final.
>
> What happens to his ranking in the tournament?
> Sections 3.1.4 and 3.3.2 of the V:EKN tournament rules
> do not entirely clarify the matter to me.
>
> This issue becomes of particular relevance in a Qualifier
> tournament. For instance, suppose there are 6 qualification
> "slots", and the player who has ended the preliminary rounds
> being 4th in the ranking cannot play the final round. Does he
> qualify or not? And what happens in the same situation if,
> say, the qualification slots are only 4?

Assuming you have more than 4 qualifying spots, the person who doesn't
play in the final retains his or her qualifying position.

If you have 4 or fewer qualifying spots, then the final round
determines who gets them, so only people who play in the final would be
eligible for those spots.

> 2) One more question about qualifier rules.
> Is it possible for a player to declare before the tournament
> starts that he does not wish to qualify, and then be treated
> the same way as an "already qualified" player (i.e. not
> counting towards the number of qualification slots)?

Yes. Such a declaration must be made before start of play on the first
round.

Ah...wouldn't 5 be the breaking point here? If the qualifying player
ranked 5th left without playing the final, the 6th ranked player takes

Messages.Body:

> > Assuming you have more than 4 qualifying spots, the person who doesn't

> >

> > determines who gets them, so only people who play in the final would be
> > eligible for those spots.
> >
>
> Ah...wouldn't 5 be the breaking point here?

No. With 5 spots available, the qualifiers are known before the finals
start.

And note that the numbers can be more lenient if previously-qualified
players go to the finals, too. If there are only 4 qualifying spots and
one previously-qualified player makes the finals, then the new
qualifiers are still known before the finals begin.

> If the qualifying player
> ranked 5th left without playing the final, the 6th ranked player takes
> his place, and if the table were to time out, everyone in the final
> would be ranked higher than the player who did not play the final.
> Only if the substitute player scored 0 vps would the absent player then
> retain his qualifying status.

Moot, but how would anyone's performance in the final change things?
Even if someone swept, all the finalist would "finish" ahead of all the
players who did not play the finals.

But (by the ruling above) that wouldn't affect the figuring of who
qualified (assuming it was known before the finals started).



I'm opposed to this. To qualify, it should be based on the standing at
the end of the final round. the end of the final round is the end of the
tournament, and it's the whole tournament that should decide who qualifies.

if I pull out after the 2nd round with two sweeps, and thus (say) I
would have been coming 1st at the end of the 3 prelim rounds, do I still
get to qualify? (If, say there are 5 qualifying spots). I'm pretty sure
dropping before the start of the third round should put me at the bottom
of the rankings, and I shouldn't get to qualify.

If this means people will hang around for 5 mins to start the final and
then "roll at his earliest convenience" to make sure they qualify, then
obviously they're not 'playing to win', should be removed from the
table, and have their ranking removed, thus not qualifying.

I can't believe people should be rewarding for not even playing the full
tournament. If they don't think they'll be able to stay the full time,
they should say so at the start and thus exclude themselves from the
qualifying spots, and if it's an emergency as to why they have to leave,
well that's unfortunate, but obviously whatever it is that's pulling
them away is more important than qualifying, and thus they shouldn't be
too upset for not qualifying (as if it was more important to qualify,
obviously this 'emergency' wouldn't pull them away).

play. all. of. the. game.

Of course the question doesn't arise except in terms of outside
concerns (catching a plane, for example).

And why penalize the player who qualified for having to catch a plane?

If there are 6 spots and the #6 player has to catch a plane (and cannot
stay to watch the finals), would you disqualify him?

What if the #5 player dropped (propelling the #6 player to the final)
-- would he then lose his qualification?

What if #6 had already left (having swept his table in 30m and already
calculating his 6p finish as his highest possible finish)? Would you
disqualify him after the fact?

Even if all of the above is acceptable to you, note that it makes
finishing 6th preferable to finishing 5th.

> I can't believe people should be rewarding for not even playing the full
> tournament.

So the late-comer shouldn't be allowed to qualify, even if he wins?
Should his tournament victory be stripped as well?

Note also that it is not a matter of rewarding them "for" not playing.
It's rewarding them for their performance in play, and not penalizing
them after the performance.

> If they don't think they'll be able to stay the full time,
> they should say so at the start and thus exclude themselves from the

Messages.Author: Bram Vink

Finals is a *whole* different ballgame than open rounds. Average level
of play and decks is seriously different. Purely open rounds would
favor agressive players who can intimidate/manipulate weaker players,
over those that have a good deck and play well. The finals is one of
the few rounds that's not significantly based on popularity.

And, if there's 5 people that qualify. Top 5 get automatically
qualified, no matter what the outcome of the finals.
If there's less than that, the finals would decide upon who'd get
qualified or not.

If someone has to cede his spot to someone, because of external
circumstances, it would seem unfair he'd have to trade his hard won
qualification that in no way was affected by the game he couldn't play.

No. F didn't qualify. The qualifiers were set when they were known --
which is after the preliminary rounds in this case.

> Conversely, same scenario with F filling in.
> E wins tournament, F gets other VPs, now ABC get 0VP in final. D does
> not qualify, correct? Since clearly, E and F came in 1st and 2nd, and
> AB and C came in 3rd 4th, and 5th respectively, unless they were tied
> going into the final.

Same thing -- the five qualifiers were ABCDE, as determined before the
finals.

See my other messages in this thread regarding a qualifier with 6 spots
to see more reasons why.

> I think I am confused, because I feel like LSJ you are saying that the
> final has no bearing on whether someone qualifies or not.

You have read correctly -- nothing to be confused about.

If there are 5 or more qualifying spots, the the qualifiers will be
known (and set) before the finals begin.

If the qualifiers are not known before the finals (that is, if you must
play the finals to determine who qualifies), then the qualifiers are
not set before the final begin, and you must play the finals to
determine who qualifies.

This can only happen when there are fewer than 5 qualifying spots
(although, depending on the number of previously-qualified players who
finish in the top 5, it may be possible in some cases to determine the
qualifiers before the final even if there are fewer than 5 spots).

http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/index.php?line=Championship

under "How to Qualify" it says:

"For championships outside of Australia, the rule is the same as last
year: The top 25% (round up) of the non-qualifed players at a
Continental Qualifier become qualified. For example, 35 players attend
a Qualifier. 2 are already qualified. So 35 - 2 = 33. 25% of 33 = 8.25.
Round up to 9. So the top 9 (not already qualified) players qualify.
The players who had already qualified before the event do not take any
of the 9 slots away from non-qualified players."

The phrase "top 25%" is I think what is tripping me up. I would assume
that in a tournament, the top 25% would at least include people scored
VPs in the finals? Even if they weren't qualified going in, but
managed to slip in because someone dropped and then scored they scored
a VP.

Unless the finals aren't actually part of the tournament for some
reason?

best -

How could you not know that if the top 7 players qualify then the
finalists (the top 5) qualify?
This is trivial to know -- it follows directly from the qualification
process description.

> > 2) In that rare case, it is better to allow the player to drop than to
> > create an artificial impetus for him to remain for the start of the
> > final and find the quickest way out of the final.
>
> Well put, but what 'impetus' is there for the substitute player to play
> the final? They cant qualify (if ranked just short of Q before the

1) It doesn't come up except rarely.
2) After having failed to qualify, the failed-to-qualify player's
options are: a) to play no more, b) to play in the finals, or c) to
play a pick-up game with other non-finalists.

If #6 doesn't like option b), or if he has already left, then the
option goes to #7 and so on.

Obviously.

> Why not just eliminate the final then, and hold more open rounds?

Because players who make the finals like to play the finals to see who
wins (where some combination of competitive spirit, bragging rights,
prizes, and ratings appeal to them).

Obviously.
